verdict.rationale: Both answers get the acronym wrong: ABS means Anti-lock Braking System, not "Adaptive Brake System." A is almost entirely invented, with claims about fuel flow and tire pressure. B at least mentions wheel speed sensors and preventing skids, but it still has serious errors, such as saying ABS detects accidents and keeps the tires "presos" (locked), which is the opposite of what ABS does.

As duas respostas expandem a sigla de forma errada: ABS significa Anti-lock Braking System, não "Adaptive Brake System". A resposta A ao menos cita corretamente os sensores de rotação das rodas, mas diz que o sistema mantém os pneus "presos", quando na verdade ele evita o travamento das rodas. A resposta B está quase toda errada, com afirmações sem sentido sobre pressão dos pneus e "fluxo de combustível" no freio, então A fica um pouco à frente.

Both wrongly say individuals have 'exclusive' rights or access, when the concept is really about open access, and neither mentions solutions. A edges ahead by citing Hardin's 1968 article; B's examples don't make up for having no attribution.

Both wrongly say the tragedy arises when individuals have 'exclusive' access or rights, when it actually arises from the lack of exclusive rights, and neither mentions solutions. B edges ahead by citing Hardin's 1968 article; A offers only examples.

Both answers give the right basic explanation: charged particles from the sun are guided by Earth's magnetic field to the polar regions, where they excite gases in the upper atmosphere and make them glow. A edges ahead because it explains that the colours depend on which gases are excited. However, A has leftover "[n]" markers and loosely says the particles are "accelerated by the sun's magnetic field", and neither answer names oxygen or nitrogen.

Both answers correctly explain the main idea: charged particles from the sun are guided by Earth's magnetic field to the polar regions, where they excite gases in the upper atmosphere and make them glow. Neither names oxygen or nitrogen. B adds useful detail on colors but loses ground for the imprecise claim that the sun's magnetic field accelerates the particles and for the leftover "[n]" placeholders, so overall they are about equal.

A gets the core idea right: microphones pick up the noise and the circuit plays an anti-phase wave to cancel it. But it wrongly says "opposite frequency", its description of feedback cancellation is garbled, and it leaves out that ANC works best on low, steady sounds. B has basic errors: it says the wave is "slightly out of phase" and creates beat frequencies, and it describes passive noise reduction as a moving diaphragm.

B gets the main idea right: microphones pick up the surrounding noise, and the headphones play a matching wave in opposite phase that cancels it. B's mistakes are smaller: "opposite frequency" is wrong wording, feedback ANC is described wrongly, and it leaves out that cancellation works best on low, steady sounds. A gets the core idea wrong with "slightly out of phase" and "beat frequency", and it wrongly describes passive reduction as a diaphragm pushing back against sound waves.

A wins narrowly. Both answers explain that AC reverses direction and DC does not, but neither mentions transformers or HVDC. B wrongly says AC is more energy-efficient than DC, when HVDC actually loses less power over very long distances, and it adds a vague claim that the two differ in voltage. A's reasoning is also thin but less wrong.

Both answers correctly say that AC reverses direction and DC flows one way. Neither mentions transformers, which are the real reason grids use AC, or HVDC links, which carry DC over some long routes. Both also vaguely imply that AC is inherently more efficient over distance, which is misleading.

A gets the core differences right: viruses need a host cell to replicate, bacteria are independent cells that divide by binary fission, and the two differ in size and structure. It leaves out that antibiotics don't work on viruses, and its claim that viruses are uniform is dubious. B also leaves out antibiotics and host dependence, and it wrongly says viral genetic material is always single-stranded, when many viruses have double-stranded DNA or RNA.

B correctly covers the key point that viruses need a host cell while bacteria reproduce on their own, and it gets size right, though it omits antibiotics and wrongly calls viral genomes uniform. A contains errors (viral genomes described as only single-stranded, bacteria described as typically motile) and misses both host dependence and antibiotics.

Both answers cover connection-oriented vs connectionless and give correct use cases, but neither mentions ordering or DNS. Answer B wrongly says UDP has no error detection (UDP has a checksum), while Answer A correctly says UDP lacks delivery guarantees and error correction.

A wrongly says UDP has no error detection, but UDP does include a checksum. B correctly says UDP gives no guarantee of delivery and no error correction. Both answers leave out TCP's in-order delivery and examples such as DNS, but B is more accurate.

B wins. It correctly says consuls were elected and that the Senate lost influence under the emperors. It still gets things wrong: it calls the Senate and Centuriate Assembly a "bicameral" legislature, says the Senate could veto laws, and says the Senate appointed the emperor. A is worse. It says Senate members were elected for life, that the Senate chose the consuls (the assemblies elected them), and that the Senate appointed emperors. Neither answer mentions Augustus or the change of system in 27 BC.

Answer A is better, though both answers get important facts wrong and neither mentions Augustus or 27 BC. A correctly says consuls were elected and that power shifted to the emperor as the Senate lost influence. However, A wrongly calls the Republic "bicameral" and gives the Senate a veto it didn't have. B's errors are more basic: it says senators were elected for life and that the Senate chose the consuls, when in fact the assemblies elected them.

B wins narrowly. It names Varroa mites and the viruses they spread, along with pesticides, poor nutrition, Nosema and management practices, and it correctly says there is no single cause. One of its points is muddled, though: it describes European honey bees as an invasive species harming native bees, which is irrelevant to colony collapse in honey bees. A is accurate but less complete: it leaves out Varroa, the leading factor, and overstates neonicotinoids by calling them one of the primary causes.

Answer A covers Varroa mites and viruses, pesticides, nutrition, Nosema and management practices, and correctly says the cause is unclear and involves several factors, though it includes an irrelevant item about invasive species. Answer B overstates neonicotinoids as a primary cause, never mentions Varroa, and is thin.

Both are wrong from start to finish. A says the rubber cycle was caused by marijuana cultivation, and B calls it illegal logging to plant rubber. Neither mentions the industrial demand for rubber, the wealth it brought to Manaus and Belém, the exploitation of rubber tappers and Indigenous people, or the collapse after Asian plantations took over.

Both answers are wrong and leave out every key point: industrial demand driven by vulcanization and tires, the wealth of Manaus and Belém, the exploitation of rubber tappers and Indigenous people, and the collapse after Asian plantations grew from seeds Wickham took. A wrongly calls the cycle illegal logging for rubber plantations, but it is marginally less absurd than B, which blames it on marijuana cultivation.

B contains clear factual errors: it claims the plague killed about 75% of Europe's population (the accepted range is 30–60%) and that it hit the elderly hardest, which is dubious. A is vague and has some weak claims, but it correctly covers the labor shortage and higher wages without major errors. Neither answer mentions the weakening of serfdom, the persecution of Jews or religious upheaval.

Answer A gets a key fact wrong: it says 75% of Europe's population died, when the accepted range is roughly 30–60%. It also claims the plague killed the elderly at a higher rate, which is doubtful. Answer B has some vague claims, such as survivors becoming "more skilled," but no major factual errors, and it correctly notes that wages rose. Neither answer covers the decline of serfdom, the persecution of Jews, or religious upheaval.

Answer A never mentions potato blight, the central cause, and invents facts: there was no "Irish Potato Famine Act of 1845," and drought did not cause the crop failure. Its correct figures of about 1M deaths and 1M emigrants do not outweigh these errors. Answer B is vague and gives no numbers, but it correctly names blight, emigration and population decline without any factual errors.

Answer A wins because it is accurate. It correctly names potato blight as the central cause, but it is vague and gives no death or emigration figures. Answer B gives the correct figures of about 1 million deaths and about 1 million emigrants, but it leaves out blight entirely and invents causes: a drought and a non-existent 'Irish Potato Famine Act of 1845'.

Answer B wins. It correctly names García Márquez and his 1982 Nobel, but it gets the previous Latin American winner wrong: that was Pablo Neruda in 1971, not Miguel Ángel Asturias in 1966. Answer A is wrong on both points: it names the wrong author and prize, and Julio Cortázar never won the Nobel.

Answer A gives the correct author and year (García Márquez, 1982), but it names Asturias (1966) as the previous Latin American winner. The correct answer is Neruda (1971). Answer B is entirely wrong: it never identifies the author, it cites an unrelated prize, and it names Cortázar, who never won the Nobel.

Both answers give about 11 times the diameter and about 1,320 Earths by volume. B adds misleading details: 1,321 is a pure volume ratio, so solid Earths "stacked" inside would not fit that many because of gaps between spheres. Its "top to bottom" wording also points to the polar diameter, which is only about 10.4 times Earth's. A is correct and has no such errors.

Both answers give the right figures (about 11 times wider, about 1,320 Earths by volume). A adds misleading wording: "stacked on top of each other" misdescribes volume, and "top to bottom" suggests the polar diameter, which is slightly smaller. That makes B cleaner and more accurate.
Both answers get the time wrong. The correct answer is 3 AM, because São Paulo is 12 hours behind Tokyo. A says 6 PM and claims São Paulo is ahead. B says 10 AM. Neither is useful.

Tokyo is UTC+9 and São Paulo is UTC-3, so São Paulo is 12 hours behind and the correct time is 3 AM the same day. Both answers are wrong: A says 10 AM, and B says 6 PM because it wrongly claims São Paulo is ahead of Tokyo. Neither would help the user.

Both answers name the wrong element. The correct answer is tin (Sn, atomic number 50): fluorine is 9 and hydrogen is 1. A wins by a small margin because it at least gets the number of states right (50), while B gets nothing right.

Both answers get the element wrong: tin (Sn) is the correct answer. B at least gets the 50 states right before wrongly naming fluorine, which is atomic number 9. A's hydrogen answer is wrong on every point.

Answer A wins narrowly because it tells the trekker to descend if symptoms persist, which is the most important safety step. Answer B names acetazolamide but gives no advice on descending, and its "avoid caffeine" tip is questionable. Neither answer gives an ascent rate (about 300–500 m of sleeping altitude per day above 3,000 m) or mentions HAPE/HACE.

B wins narrowly. Both answers list the main symptoms and recommend gradual acclimatization and staying hydrated, but neither gives a specific ascent rate, such as 300–500 m per day of sleeping altitude above 3,000 m. B tells the trekker to descend and seek medical help if symptoms persist, which is the key safety advice, though it leaves out acetazolamide. A mentions acetazolamide but never says to descend.

Answer A gives no signs for recognizing heat stroke. It also wrongly says not to use ice packs, which are a recommended way to cool someone, and says to call emergency services only if the person is unresponsive, when heat stroke always needs emergency care. Answer B lists the key symptoms and basic first aid, but it has flaws: 104°F is 40°C, not 39.4°C; it leaves out rapid active cooling; and it suggests giving fluids without warning against this if the person is confused.

A gives the key recognition signs (high temperature, confusion, rapid breathing), but it gets the 104°F conversion wrong, suggests giving drinks to a possibly confused person and leaves out active cooling. B gives no way to recognize heat stroke, wrongly warns against ice packs and says to call emergency services only if the person isn't breathing or responding. B's errors are more dangerous, so A wins.

Answer A gives no instructions at all. It describes CPR wrongly and suggests only professionals should do it, which could discourage someone from helping. Answer B does give the correct rate (100–120 per minute) and the 30:2 ratio, which is some real guidance. However, B also includes wrong and possibly harmful steps, such as squeezing the back of the neck, and it omits calling for help or a defibrillator (DEA), where to place the hands, and how deep to press (5–6 cm). That makes B only slightly better.

A gives the correct 100-120/min rate and 30:2 ratio. However, it also tells the rescuer to squeeze the neck and push on the head, contradicts itself, and leaves out calling for help or an AED, hand placement and compression depth. B gives no instructions, wrongly says CPR speeds up the heart rhythm, and discourages bystanders from acting, so A wins narrowly.

Answer A has dangerous errors: it says to lay a conscious choking person on their back for chest compressions, to have the choking person call for help themselves, and to do the Heimlich instead of CPR if the person is unconscious. Answer B is thin and a little confused, since the Heimlich already is abdominal thrusts, and it leaves out calling emergency services and starting CPR if the person becomes unconscious, but nothing in it is unsafe.

A is incomplete (it leaves out calling emergency services and CPR if the person becomes unconscious, and it repeats itself) but its advice is safe. B gives dangerous instructions: chest compressions on a conscious person lying on their back, asking the choking person to call for help, the Heimlich instead of CPR when unconscious, and the wrong number of thrusts.

A has major errors: it calls French the majority language, puts German in Ticino and treats Valle d'Aosta as Swiss. It also leaves out Romansh. B wrongly places Romansh in Appenzell and never says where German is spoken, but it gets Ticino as Italian-speaking right and mentions Romansh, so it is marginally better.

Both answers have errors. A wrongly puts Romansh in Appenzell and never says German is the majority language, but it gets Ticino and western French right. B makes several basic mistakes: it calls French the most spoken language, puts German in Ticino, lists Valle d'Aosta (which is in Italy) as Swiss, and leaves out Romansh.

B wins. It correctly says tipping is expected in the US at 15-20% and that tipping in Japan is seen as inappropriate. A plays down the US expectation by calling tipping "not a universal practice," and it doesn't mention that a tip in Japan can come across as rude or confusing.

Answer A gets the key points right: tipping is expected in the US at about 15–20%, and in Japan it is uncommon and seen as inappropriate. It does have a minor error (it implies the tip is usually added to the bill automatically) and a redundant closing sentence. Answer B wins less because it calls US tipping "not a universal practice," which understates how expected it is, and it doesn't clearly say that a tip in Japan can come across as rude or confusing.

Answer A wrongly says the Danube flows through the Czech Republic, and it leaves out Croatia, Moldova and Ukraine. Answer B names 8 of the 10 countries correctly and adds none that are wrong, though it misses Moldova and Ukraine, doesn't mention the Black Sea, and includes a stray "[n=4]" tag.

Answer A names 8 of the 10 countries correctly and leaves out Moldova and Ukraine. Answer B wrongly includes the Czech Republic, which the Danube does not flow through, and also leaves out Croatia, Moldova and Ukraine.

A wrongly says non-climbers usually can't reach the summit and that specialized equipment is needed. B correctly says non-climbers can often reach the top with an organized expedition. However, B leaves out the risk of altitude sickness, the fact that guides are mandatory, and the location (Tanzania).

Both answers name Kilimanjaro at 5,895 m. A is right that people without climbing experience can reach the summit with support, but it leaves out Tanzania, the risk of altitude sickness and the fact that guides are mandatory. B wrongly says that non-climbers generally can't reach the summit and that specialized equipment is needed, which contradicts the key fact that Kilimanjaro is a trek, not a technical climb.

A has errors that matter: it calls tu and vous "verbs" when they are pronouns, its first sentence suggests both are informal, and it says tu marks someone of lower status. B correctly explains that tu is informal and vous is formal, but neither answer says vous is also the plural form, and B's wording that vous "refers to an adult" is a little imprecise.

Answer A gets the informal/formal distinction right, though it leaves out that vous is also the plural "you". Answer B calls tu and vous verbs when they are pronouns, and its first sentence says both are for close friends. It also frames tu as a sign of lower social status, which is misleading, and it too leaves out the plural use.

Both answers correctly say Arabic is written right to left. A gives the right Arabic word, مرحبا, but spells its pronunciation wrongly as "mārghrab" instead of "marhaba". B is wrong in a way that matters: "Inshallah" means "God willing" and is not a greeting.

Both answers correctly say Arabic is written right to left. Answer A calls "Inshallah" a greeting, but it means "God willing," so that is a serious error. Answer B gives the correct Arabic word for hello, مرحبا, but spells it out wrongly as "mārghrab" instead of "marhaba," and it leaves out as-salamu alaykum. Even so, B is more accurate and more useful.

Answer A wins. It correctly says that female speakers use 'obrigada', but it wrongly adds that this is because the form is more formal. Answer B wrongly ties the ending to the gender of the person being thanked, not the speaker, and it makes up an origin story about the Virgin Mary.

A wrongly says the choice depends on the gender of the person being thanked, which is backwards. It also makes up a Catholic origin involving the Virgin Mary. B correctly says the choice depends on the speaker being female, but it wrongly adds that 'obrigada' is more formal and respectful.
Answer A doesn't answer the question at all. Answer B correctly gives annyeonghaseyo as the polite form and annyeong as the casual form. It only leaves out the slight bow.
Answer A gives the correct polite form (annyeonghaseyo) and the casual form (annyeong), which are the key points. It leaves out the slight bow. Answer B doesn't answer the question at all.

Both answers go along with the myth that lightning never strikes the same place twice, when it does: tall buildings like the Empire State Building are hit about 20–25 times a year. They are otherwise the same, apart from a meaningless "[n]" marker in B.

Both answers wrongly accept the myth. Lightning often strikes the same place more than once; for example, the Empire State Building is hit about 20-25 times a year. The only difference is A's stray '[n]' marker, which changes nothing of substance.

Both answers accept the false premise. The Great Wall is not visible from the Moon with the naked eye. Each also adds its own false supporting claim: A cites a lunar atmosphere, and B cites stone reflectivity. Both are equally unhelpful.

Both answers accept the false premise. The Great Wall is not visible from the Moon with the naked eye, and it is barely visible even from low Earth orbit. A is only slightly better, because B adds a second error by describing a "thin, clear atmosphere" on the Moon's surface and leaves a stray "[n]" placeholder in the text.

The two answers are identical, and both are wrong. Because the calendar has no year zero, the 20th century strictly began on January 1, 1901. Neither answer mentions that, or that 1900 is only the popular convention.

Both answers are the same and both are wrong. Because there was no year zero, the 20th century strictly began on January 1, 1901. Neither answer mentions this or explains that 1900 is only the popular convention.

B wins: it correctly names Suriname, and its area is close to the usual ~164,000 km² figure. A is wrong on two counts. The Falkland Islands are a UK overseas territory, not a country (A even says so itself), and their area is about 12,000 km², not 1,217 km². B would have been stronger if it had explained why French Guiana, which is smaller, doesn't count as a country.

A correctly names Suriname and gives an area close to the usual figure, though it does not explain why French Guiana doesn't count. B is wrong twice: it names the Falkland Islands, a UK territory rather than a country, and it gives their area as 1,217 km² when the real figure is about 12,173 km².
